newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch and French call truce, sign anti-drugs pact.
newsitem.headline: Dutch and French call truce, sign anti-drugs pact.

text.p: The Netherlands and France set aside their differences over drugs policy on Monday and agreed to work closely together to stamp out drug-smuggling.

Ministers from both countries signed an agreement which will also step up cooperation between the two national customs services in the fight against illegal trafficking in weapons, protected plants and animals and counterfeit goods.

The conciliatory tone struck by French Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure and Dutch Finance Secretary Willem Vermeend was in sharp contrast to the war of words which has flared up between the two countries from time to time in recent years.
France has accused the Dutch of pursusing a lax policy under which young people from other European countries have easy access to cheap drugs which they then circulate at home.
The Netherlands, meanwhile, has accused France of trying to dictate Dutch domestic policy and of being blind to the positive results it says have been achieved by "decriminalising" drugs.
But there were no recriminations on Monday as the ministers adopted a friendlier tone, for the time being at least.
"I really think that this agreement will contribute to better relations between both countries," Vermeend said.
Vermeend said an extensive exchange of information between the two countries would form the cornerstone of the agreement.
Binational customs teams will be formed both on an ad-hoc and a permanent basis, building on the experience gained with such teams in the ports of Marseilles and Rotterdam.
Rotterdam will also follow the example of Le Havre in installing scanners which enable customs officers to check whether cargo containers hold illicit goods.
However, Lamassoure said France would maintain border checks in the north for the time being despite agreements within Europe to remove such obstacles to the movement of people and goods.
The French minister said this was not only to deter drug smugglers, but also because France faced a "terrorist threat".
